blocks.text: Next, the essential teaching as explained, in four parts. First, the account of the sutra's name; second, the account of the sutra's substance; third, the account of its cardinal purport; fourth, the account of its function and power. The expression and the expressed lie within these four, so they are gathered and set forth in order to exhaust the purport of the whole sutra. One may well call him a person thoroughly versed in the Great Vehicle. Now first, the account of the sutra's name.

inline.s: [Commentary] He opens the vow-gate of the dharma-treasury and points to the wonderful land of the Land of Bliss.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra fully sets forth the retribution-body and the environment, together with the assemblies, and these are the expression that names it; yet the sutra-title says only 'The Buddha speaks of Amitabha.' As the Great Master's commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: 'Raise the proper retribution to gather in the dependent fruition, and describe the teaching lord to include the assemblies.' That is to say, the title speaks only of the proper, raising the proper to gather in the dependent; the preface speaks only of the dependent, raising the dependent to gather in the proper. This cross-reference is the craft of the composition. As for this sutra not expounding the opening of the vow-gate, it is because the Larger Sutra states it in detail, and so it is omitted here.

blocks.text: Next, the account of the sutra's substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] The bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source; the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.

[Sub-commentary] 'The bejeweled groves and jade-like pools' briefly raises the dependent retribution of which the sutra speaks, from the passage on the seven rows of railings down to the jeweled trees and jeweled nets emitting subtle sounds—one section of the scripture. 'The measure of longevity and the light' briefly raises the proper retribution of which it speaks, from the passage 'For what reason is that Buddha named Amitabha' down to 'It can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas'—another section. 'Directly reveal the mind-source; fully manifest the self-nature'—these two lines properly describe its substance. For this sutra takes the seal of reality as its proper substance: the formless yet all-formed, the formed yet formless, is called real-form. Now the bejeweled groves and jade-like pools, the measure of longevity and the light, are certainly the characteristics of all dharmas; yet if they directly reveal the mind-source and fully manifest the self-nature, what characteristic can be obtained? This is precisely the proper substance of the formless-yet-formed and the formed-yet-formless. The wonderful teaching of a Pure Land that is the mind and an Amitabha that is the self-nature is easy to utter but hard to make precise; one who would profoundly apprehend its purport must arrive at what is most fitting. If one seeks to clarify it, the Tiantai teaching of the dharma-nature alone suffices. Why? The Land of Bliss lies far beyond a hundred thousand ko?i of lands, and Amitabha Buddha is a person of fruit, complete in wisdom and severance and pure in fulfillment. An ordinary being of the ordinary ground, defiled by the three delusions and sunk in the two deaths, creating inexhaustible karma-entanglements and making never-ending causes of birth, how could he suddenly respond to Amitabha, be reborn in the Pure Land, cut across the five destinies, and at once reach non-retrogression? It is precisely because in this school's exposition the dharma-nature of living beings has three meanings. First, the nature's measure: it pervades the ten directions and interpenetrates with nothing outside—the Land of Bliss beyond a hundred thousand ko?i of lands is within our nature's measure only a close-adjacent corner. Second, the nature's substance: what is everlastingly constant and firmly set, pure and luminous—Amitabha's wisdom and severance, the complete awakened substance—corresponds to our nature's substance ultimately and without difference. Third, the nature's endowment: but if one speaks only of 'nothing outside' and 'no difference' without understanding the gateway of the nature's endowment, then though one says 'nothing outside,' in the end there remains an outside, and though one says 'no difference,' in the end there remains a difference. Nor would one know from what cause the virtue of the nature's measure and substance is pervasive, or by what means it is pure. Know that there is the endowment of the nature: then what was before called the virtue of substance and the virtue of measure all have the nature's endowment as their root. The purport of the three natures is fully set out in the Treatise on Birth and Non-birth, and is not enumerated at length here.

blocks.text: Third, the account of the cardinal purport.

inline.s: [Commentary] The assembly of many sages abide in one place; it is not by small virtue that one is reborn there. Holding the name for seven days lies in the single-mindedness that is unconfused.

[Sub-commentary] Hereafter, in the explanation of the title's five sections, faith, vows, and the pure karma are taken as the cardinal purport of the whole sutra. Now, gathering the scripture and giving a brief account, it speaks only of the pure karma, because among the three essentials this is the proper one. The first line corresponds to the scripture's 'That Buddha has immeasurable, unbounded shravaka disciples, all arhats, beyond the reach of calculation; the host of bodhisattvas are likewise.' Again it says, 'Of those reborn in the Land of Bliss, all are avivartika [non-retrogressing]; many among them are in a single lifetime destined to Buddhahood, their number impossible to calculate, and can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas.' Again it says, 'Living beings who hear this should make the vow to be reborn in that land. Why? Because they may gather in one place with such hosts of superior good people.' The second line corresponds to the scripture's 'It cannot be by small roots of goodness and the causes and conditions of merit that one is reborn in that land.' Hence 'the assembly of many sages abide in one place; it is not by small virtue that one is reborn there.' The third and fourth lines correspond to the scripture's 'If there be good men and good women who hear of Amitabha Buddha and hold fast to his name, for one day, for two days, and up to seven days, single-minded and unconfused.' Precisely because the bejeweled groves and the jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source, and the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature, and because living beings from beginningless time, through the causes and conditions of dullness and movement, have drifted through the five turbidities and cannot return to the one true—now when they are about to return to the root and revert to the source, nothing precedes illuminating the dullness and stilling the movement. Holding the name for seven days is what illuminates its dullness; single-minded and unconfused is what stills its movement. When dullness and movement are both forgotten, what is there to await for the true? It is like dust cleared and the mirror bright, the wind quieted and the waves still. Yet that the mere holding of the name for seven days should at once reach non-retrogression shows precisely that the teaching belongs to the Round and the Sudden—that without waiting a single lifetime, the profound power of the vows, the compassion that gives and takes away, and the fundamental merit-power are inconceivable. This is truly the vital ford that quickly escapes birth-and-death and the highway of the bodhisattva's practice.

blocks.text: Fourth, the account of the function and power, in two parts. First, the proper statement of the function and power.

inline.s: [Commentary] Matters and principle are one in substance; living beings and the Buddha are originally the same. The compassion that is without conditions responds without forethought.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra takes the leaving of suffering and the attainment of joy as its function. That is, the scripture says: 'When that person's life comes to an end, Amitabha Buddha with the hosts of sages appear before him. When that person ends, his mind is not inverted, and he immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.' Thus the function and power of this sutra concern the giving and the taking away. The work of giving and taking away lies in the response and the sensing. Living beings, with single-minded holding of the name, form the sensing; Amitabha, with the taking away of suffering and the bestowal of joy, forms the response. The way of taking away suffering is grounded in compassion, and the way of bestowing joy is grounded in kindness; both are the natural relation of the essential nature, not in the least forced. The practitioner takes as his sensing the way that matters and principle are one in substance and living beings and the Buddha are fundamentally the same; Amitabha takes as his response the way that the unconditioned compassion responds without forethought. Is it not then that Amitabha, by coming without coming, comes to this Saha to receive and guide the practitioner; and the practitioner, by going without going, goes to that Land of Bliss to behold and bow to Amitabha? This is truly the rational basis on which the function and power of this sutra rely.

blocks.text: Next, the merit and works that are brought forth.

inline.s: [Commentary] Realizing the originally complete in the mind, the countless lands are not far; knowing that the great vows may be relied upon, the three asamkhya kalpas are cut across transversely.

[Sub-commentary] The foregoing already made clear the rational basis of the function and power. Relying on it to invoke the Buddha and seek rebirth: one who can realize that matters and principle are one in substance and living beings and the Buddha are fundamentally the same, then the far region of the hundred thousand ko?i of lands is all the originally complete of my own mind—though far, it is not far. One who can know that the unconditioned compassion responds without forethought, then the forty-eight great vows are unconditionally reliable, and the stream of consciousness can be cut across. Such is the function and power—is it not surpassing? As for 'cutting across the three asamkhya kalpas': this shows that transcending the three realms has both a vertical and a horizontal sense. According to the Abhidharma, a bodhisattva of the Tripitaka through three asamkhya kalpas practices the six perfections and the myriad practices, plants for a hundred kalpas the cause of the marks of excellence, and then reaches non-retrogression and attains the fivefold dharma-body. This is the vertical exit, ascending from below to above, like a rabbit or a horse crossing a river in a winding, lengthy way. But those who, in accordance with this sutra, seek rebirth in the Land of Bliss—whether already reborn, currently reborn, or to be reborn—all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Again it says, 'Those reborn there are all avivartika.' This is the horizontal exit, reaching the other shore directly from here, like the fragrant elephant cutting across the stream—attained in a single thought. Hence this function and power is the most excellent.

blocks.text: Next, the reason for the brief annotation, in two parts. First, the proper account, in three parts. First, the reason for the broad explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture is concise and the Buddha's intent is profound and subtle; though recitation and upholding are many, careful study is truly rare.

[Sub-commentary] This sutra does not exceed a thousand words, yet it fully expresses the purport of a Pure Land that is the mind and an Amitabha that is the self-nature. One may truly say the scripture is concise and the Buddha's intent profound and subtle. Moreover, the World-honored Amitabha is especially related to the Saha beings, so that those who hear this teaching all accept it with joy and reverence. Add to this that the sutra's words are simple and its practice easy, and it meets the capacity of beings for easy faith; hence both clergy and laity recite, read, and uphold it. Yet the text being clear is easy to glimpse, while the principle being deep is rarely investigated; this causes the Buddha's intent to be obscured and not revealed. Then the explanations of the former worthies could not but be broad.

blocks.text: Next, the reason for the brief explanation.

inline.s: [Commentary] Only the writings of the former worthies are lamented as rarely heard by the later ages.

[Sub-commentary] The writings of the former worthies are listed separately after the preface. Masters such as Ci'en and Gushan each had their compositions—some with expansive words, some with profound and subtle principles, all unbefitting the first-stage practitioner; hence they are rarely heard in later ages. Therefore the present brevity cannot but be put forth.

blocks.text: Third, the proper account of the brief explanation, in two parts. First, the account of the modest spirit.

inline.s: [Commentary] Presumptuously imitating the circulation of the teaching, I briefly set forth my citations.

[Sub-commentary] 'Circulation': the Golden Light commentary says, 'Flowing is the name of pouring down; circulating is the name of not being blocked.' The wish is that the water of the right Dharma should, from this present time, pour down to the future, and that the trap and the net of the holy teachings should not be blocked in ages to come. The Great Master speaks humbly: privately I have imitated the ancients in circulating the great Dharma, and therefore briefly set forth my citations, drawing on the established words of the various explanations to form the brief explanation. Yet in the process I sometimes use the meaning without the wording, abbreviate the expression but not the intent, in order to complete a single school's utterance, as if it came from one person's pen—one may call this a felicitous mode of authorship.

blocks.text: Next, the account of his own vow.

inline.s: [Commentary] I wish, with like-minded companions, universally to bind the pure affinity and all to realize non-birth, together ascending to non-retrogression. Such is my humble claim.

[Sub-commentary] The first two lines present a private understanding for the benefit of others—binding with like-minded companions the pure affinity of the Buddha's land broadly. The next two lines apply one's own aspiration to all beings—according to those who hear, to realize and ascend to the station of non-birth and non-retrogression. This is precisely the bodhisattva's resolve to benefit self and others, the mind of the awakened one's great compassion in its vast succor.

[Commentary] The Tang Master Ci'en composed a Comprehensive Praise of Amitabha in one scroll; the Song masters Gushan, Jingjue, and Lingzhi each had commentaries and notes; the masters Lun of Sanqu and Xin of Gu'ai each wrote collected annotations. Now wishing to follow the brief for the ease of first-stage practitioners, I set them aside separately, each following his own intent.

[Sub-commentary] 'The Tang Master Ci'en' onwards sets forth the ancients' annotations; 'now wishing to follow the brief' onwards sets forth his own annotation. Since this sutra is so widely recited, the annotations and commentaries must be many. Those now cited, that fall within my reading and hearing, are only the six masters by count. Those I have recently seen further include the sectioned commentary of Master Zong Yuexi, the sectioned explanation of Master Puzhi in the Hongwu period of the present dynasty, and the commentary-annotation of the recent Master Lianchi. If the brief is to be followed, this explanation is the most so. As for wishing wide reading, that too is to be followed by each according to his own intent.
